Chapters.Title: Setting off
Chapters.Text: During the four years of my PhD I spent a lot of time dreaming of vanlife, and watching a lot of youtube videos for inspiration. On the 13th of July 2019 I bought a Mercedes Sprinter (long wheel base) for £7,000. It had been used as a delivery van previously and had 160k miles on the clock but was in good condition. I converted it into a campervan by cladding the interior with pine, cutting holes in the sides for windows, and putting in beds, a kitchen, electric (solar powered) and storage spaces. I built a composting toilet and fitted some back seats for the children which I picked up from a guy who was taking them out of an old minivan, also for a camper conversion. In October that year we finally set off, planning to travel the whole of Europe — if only we'd known covid was coming!

Photos.Title: Here We Go!
Photos.Description: After three years dreaming of this moment, and three months kitting out Uncle Vanya, we were finally ready to leave! Here we are in Sheffield just before setting off in October 2019, hoping to get to sunny Spain before the cold weather arrived.

Photos.Title: Denge Sound Mirrors
Photos.Description: After a long drive down to the south coast in one go we stopped the night near Denge: our first over-night in Vanya. We had our final taste of British cuisine from a fish'n'chip shop and the next day went to have a look at the Sound Mirrors. These were built during WWI to amplify the sound of approaching German planes and would become redundant with the later invention of radar, a little piece of history and science we'd not heard about before and definitely worth a visit.

Photos.Title: White Cliffs of Dover
Photos.Description: Leaving Britain! We've been on a lot of ferry journeys and not always in the best weather, but leaving from Dover on a clear, sunny day is fantastic: we watch the white cliffs disappear behind us and crowd the front of the ship waiting for the first sight of France, of the continent.

Chapters.Title: A España
Chapters.Text: We drove down to the south coast in one go with a Dover-Calais ferry booked. We were giving a lift to a friend of ours who's parents lived near Düsseldorf so we passed quickly through France, Belgium and The Netherlands, stopping for a few ours at Doel (near Antwerp), an abandoned town covered with street art. After Düsseldorf we headed through Luxembourg and down through France to Andorra.

Photos.Title: Doel, Belgium
Photos.Description: The village of Doel, an island until the 18th century, has been threatened with demolition since 1965 to make room for an expansion of the port of Antwerp. Plans have been halted indefinitely because a handful of villagers have refused to leave, meaning the village is mostly abandoned and a perfect canvas for street artists. After the ferry journey, and then the drive from Calais, we spent a great afternoon exploring here.

Photos.Title: Wildpark Düsseldorf Grafenberg
Photos.Description: We stayed with a friend of ours near Düsseldorf for a few days before heading further south and he took us to this wildlife park with dear, boar and many other animals.

Photos.Title: Düsseldorf
Photos.Description: We have visited Köln and Bochum before but out tick-list of Nordrhein-Westfalen cities was missing Düsseldorf. We had a great time there exploring the city and ended up sat outside a bar at a long table eating German bread with mustard.

Photos.Title: K21
Photos.Description: We love the K21 art gallery in Düsseldorf, we always love interactive art! On our visit several huge wire nets were suspended from the ceiling with a two-storey drop beneath. Definitely one of the more trilling exhibits we've ever seen and loads of fun.

Photos.Title: Wuppertal
Photos.Description: Leaving Düsseldorf after a couple of nights we first drove to Wuppertal, famous for its suspended monorail train system which once carried a baby elephant. The elephant apparently fell through the floor of the train into the river, but it was not seriously hurt. Fortunately, the floor held out for us as we rode the train not to get anywhere in particular but just to experience it.

Photos.Title: Neroth
Photos.Description: Probably one of the strangest towns we've been to in Germany, its claim the fame being its former status as a capital of mousetrap manufacturing. The traps were made mainly by women at home, and most of the men in the town became traveling mousetrap salesmen. The town is full of mousetrap memorials, most notably the mousetrap museum.

Photos.Title: Luxembourg
Photos.Description: We didn't spend long in Luxembourg but we saw the main sights of the capital city, Luxembourg, then spent the afternoon in the huge municipal park and playground. The children liked the clown-shaped water fountain.

Photos.Title: Metz
Photos.Description: Finally entering France we found ourselves, after a couple of days, in Metz. The main things I remember are the Centre Pompidou-Metz designed by Shigeru Ban with its undulating roof and —when we were there— life-sized bust of King Kong; and also a local skate park where I fell flat on my back merely walking around — I was in pain for about a week after and it is clear that I should work on being able to walk first before I ever take up skateboarding.

Photos.Title: Musée Cinéma et Miniature, Lyon
Photos.Description: This is a real gem of Lyon. The museum was started by artist Dan Ohlmann who made miniature scenes to be used in wide-shots in films and houses loads of his amazingly detailed creations. But it also features his huge collection of Hollywood memorabilia: the alien from Alien, the hoverboard from Back to the Future, one of the letters addressed to Harry Potter Under The Stairs, prosthetics from Nutty Professor II: The Klumps (that seminal triumph of film-making), and so much more. We were not expecting it to be as fascinating as it was and were blown away.

Photos.Title: Campfire
Photos.Description: Our first campfire! Driving up-hill to a scenic spot just outside of Lyon we were only looking for somewhere to park discretely to spend the night, but we the picnic area turned out to have a fireplace: good job we had a saw and axe to chop up some fallen branches. When picturing #Vanlife, this is what I had in mind.

Photos.Title: Palais Idéal
Photos.Description: I really find it hard to describe this place, it's something which has to be seen to be appreciated. Ferdinand "Facteur" Cheval, a local postman, had a vision of an ideal palace in a dream after tripping on an interestingly shaped rock along his route. He then spent the rest of his entire life collecting more rocks and constructing this palace with inspiration from Indian and European architecture he saw in magazines. There are thousands of quirky figurines, hand-carved messages and staircases throughout.

Photos.Title: Carcassonne
Photos.Description: We couldn't resist stopping off at Carcassonne, being fans of the board game.

Chapters.Title: De Brava a Blanca
Chapters.Text:
My first view of Spain came with blue skies and sunshine as we headed down the Pyrenees into Catalunya. Just hours after being wrapped up warm for the cold and cloud of Andorra la Vella we were sitting in the sun at a café in Montserrat, and the next day lying on the beach in Badalona. 
In one month we traveled from the Catalonian Costa Brava down along Costa Dorada, through Deltebre, ventured inland of the Valencian Community, spent some time in Valencia itself, and continued down to Alicante. 
We drank wine and beer, and ate churros, in local cafés; we experienced wild swimming in thermally heated rivers and pools; we saw forrests, mountains and beaches. What an introduction to the country!

Photos.Title: Monistrol de Montserrat
Photos.Description: Our first stop in Spain, beautiful blue skies, beautiful mountains: a great introduction. We tried ordering in Spanish for the first time: "Un café por favor" and got back: "Speak Catalan or English, we don't speak Spanish here", so we were also introduced to the politics!

Photos.Title: Beach at Badalona
Photos.Description: Finally made it to the Mediterranean Coast, albeit a fairly industrial stretch. We just stopped here a few hours to sit on the beach before heading off: since that time we've been to hundreds of hugely varied beaches along the Spanish south coast but the sight of the sea after weeks inland is always magical.

Photos.Title: People Towers at Granollers
Photos.Description: This Catalonian tradition was our first taste of the spectacular and often dangerous world of Fiesta. Coming from England —where we do trick-or-treat, maybe put out some decorations at Christmas and occasionally hang some bunting round the streets for Gay Pride or a royal jubilee— Spanish Fiesta can be overwhelming. They're regular, intense and often crazy. Building ten-person tall human towers with no safety net and a small child balancing on top is definitely one of the wildest!

Photos.Title: Cova Negra
Photos.Description: Hammock, campfire, watched Tarzan. Cave with ancient cave paintings.

Photos.Title: Parque Natural de la Serra de Mariola

Chapters.Title: December in Spain
Chapters.Text: From Alicante we carried on down the coast to Almería then headed inland to Tabernas Desert, the location of many "American" westerns, which has since become one of our favourite places in the world. From there we drove along to Granada, found a few more thermally-heated pools and then headed back down to the Costa Del Sol for Christmas on a secluded beach near Nerja where where we were able to lie in the sun and swim in the sea. Naked. In December.

Photos.Title: Secret Waterfall at Salto de Usero

Chapters.Title: South-west Iberia
Chapters.Text: We spent the week around New Year's 2019/20 in Sheffield, flying from Málaga airport. After getting back to Málaga we found we'd missed King's Day: we didn't know about it at the time, but we now look forward to it every year. We spent the next couple of months around the South West of the peninsula, bouncing between Spain and Portugal, visiting Cádiz, Sevilla, Faro, Lisbon and loads of smaller places. We went down to Tarifa for the first time and saw Africa across the water, tantilisingly close; we went to Sagres in Portugal, the south-west tip of Continental Europe. Finally, we started hearing rumors about some pandemic somewhere far away; living in a van with limited internet access we weren't really sure of the situation: everything seemed fine to us, no zombies anywhere, then one day we pulled up to a campsite and the gate was locked despite there being campers inside. A woman came up to the gate wearing a mask and told us to go away, and that was that.

Photos.Title: Parque Natural da Serra da Estrela
Aveiro
Photos.Description: Last stop before lockdown. we wandered around and looked at the beautiful boats, but things were getting weird. We were parked next to a hotel and we saw the staff carrying out dozens of matresses to be burned. It's a charming little place though.

Photos.Title: Camping Orbitur Vagueira
Photos.Description: Our last night before lockdown. We had heard things were getting serious and decided to head to a nearby campsite to have our bi-monthly showers and assess the options. The campsite told us that the next morning they would be closing the gates: if you were inside, you were going to stay inside; if you left in the morning, you wouldn't be getting back it for a while. And at that time nobody knew how long it would be. On the one hand, we didn't want to be stuck on a campsite for, potentially, months. But on the other hand, we didn't want to be arrested or told to go back to the UK — both posibilities if we continued our nomadic life while everyone else was locked-down indoors. It didn't take long for us to make up our minds: those would be our last showers for a very long time!

Photos.Title: Prettycamp Wannachill
Photos.Description: Leaving Camping Oributur and knowing that we were breaking the law just by being on the road, we were in a difficult position. The useful aire at Praia da Vagueira was roped off to prevent people like us from camping, so we headed to the nearest beach we could find which was somewhat away from civilisation: Praia de Mira, just north of the town, with nobody else around. This became our home from the 22nd of March to 19th of May: we dubbed it "Prettycamp Wannachill". The locals of Praia de Mira would walk by occasionally to walk their dogs in defiance of the lockdown: in England a troupe of foreign gypsies would have been shouted out of town, but in Portugal everyone waved and smiled, asked (from a distance) if we were ok, and even if we would like to come to their house to do laundry (we declined, obviously).

Photos.Title: Postboxes on the main road
Photos.Description: For two months we stayed on the same beach. We walked north along the beach, sometimes we walked south about 100 yards to the edge of the town, and sometimes we walked up Rua Principal—teh amin road which goes as far up as Gafanha do Carmo. This photo is a selection of the postboxes of Rua Principal, probably the most cultural thing we saw during those two months.

Photos.Title: Robot
Photos.Description: Found an old building, did some artwork.

Photos.Title: Luxury Air BnB in Coimbra
Photos.Description: There was an odd week at the start of May when it seemed that lockdown was winding down, a couple of weeks before it officially lifted. We didn't miss the opportunity to book an apartment for the night and to have a bit of luxury. Coimbra is a really nice little university town and we have revisited since. We walked around the town and the Jardins da Quinta das Lágrimas, and bought a folding bike from Decathlon which could fit in the back of the van.

Photos.Title: Lockdown is over!
Photos.Description: Once we felt safe enough to leave Prettycamp Wannachill we drove up to Estarreja where we found a fully-equiped aire, free to stay for 48 hours. The children's playground was roped off but there were a few cafes open. This would not be the end of lockdown: over the next year there would be on-and-off periods of restricted movement, but it really felt like the world was working again. Our journey back to the UK had begun.

Photos.Title: Capela do Senhor da Pedra
Photos.Description: A nice little chappel on the beach, just south of Porto.

Photos.Title: Barcelos Cock
Photos.Description: After years of familiarity with that cock from the nandos sauce bottles we finally visited his home town! Ledgend says that a Galician, who was passing through Barcelos on a pilgrimage, was falsely accused of steeling some silver and sentenced to death by hanging. He pointed to a roasted rooster on the dinner table and said "If I am innocent, the rooster will crow when I am hanged". A little while later the dead rooster got up and started crowing, so they all ran to the gallows where the Galician was not dead because the knot hadn't been tied properly. They all belived him and let him go on his way.

Photos.Title: Capbreton bunkers
Photos.Description: Back in France! It's been a while.

Photos.Title: Sitting on a hand in Angoulême
Photos.Description: Our first time in Angoulême. A few years later we came back here and completely forgot we'd been before. Wes Anderson was here to film The French Dispatch.
